notes: Fanon’s opposition to bourgeois single-party intimidation and extreme decentralisation are not replaced with a generic Leninist institutional model. Cooperative nationalisation differs from a corrupt central bureaucracy. Anti-colonial violence does not establish racial heredity or unrestricted conquest. EFF material establishes reception, not the whole foundational doctrine. Checked all 240 literal statements and agreement directions, the 15 independent axis briefs, counter-evidence, source references, period, metadata and inferred uncertainty. All 240 responses remain conservatively marked inferred; exact IDs are in the separate review. Technical validation cannot certify the historical or political estimates. Similarity decisions are added only after checking calculated neighbours.

neutralResponses.rationale: Educated assumption: Neutral is the most likely response by Fanonism in Fanon’s anti-colonial humanist and participatory programme, 1952–1961 to “Public institutions should organise their schedules around one common cultural calendar rather than accommodate different communities’ celebrations.”. Subject-specific context: National culture develops through popular struggle and solidarity rather than fixed racial essences. Counter-evidence and limits: Shared national consciousness matters; Fanon criticises both empty cosmopolitan imitation and chauvinist ethnic rivalry. Common administration and recognition of distinct celebrations compete. The specified mechanism combines competing aims in this record; a mixed response is chosen for that substantive conflict, not merely because exact evidence is unavailable. This is a contextual estimate with uncertainty, not a documented answer to this exact statement.

axes.evidence: Mass political education and decentralised popular authority oppose a leader-centred single-party bourgeois dictatorship.
axes.counterEvidence: A revolutionary party guides mobilisation; Fanon does not supply a complete contemporary constitutional code.

axes.evidence: Freedom from colonial policing and intimidation favours civil participation with protection from domination.
axes.counterEvidence: Liberation can involve coercive armed struggle; modern preventive and health mechanisms are explicit analogies, not quoted policy.

axes.evidence: National culture develops through popular struggle and solidarity rather than fixed racial essences.
axes.counterEvidence: Shared national consciousness matters; Fanon criticises both empty cosmopolitan imitation and chauvinist ethnic rivalry.

axes.evidence: His criticism of expelling other Africans and racial-national exclusion favours mobility and solidarity.
axes.counterEvidence: This is an extension of anti-chauvinism; a contemporary visa and housing programme is not specified.

axes.evidence: Armed liberation from colonial domination is compatible with human solidarity and opposition to imperial conquest.
axes.counterEvidence: Revolutionary violence is not support for every overseas campaign or automated weapon; those mechanisms remain qualified estimates.

axes.evidence: National liberation should develop into African and human solidarity rather than bourgeois chauvinism.
axes.counterEvidence: Colonial international domination is rejected; independent self-determination is not automatic delegation to existing global institutions.

axes.evidence: Cooperative nationalisation puts resources and intermediary trade at the service of the people.
axes.counterEvidence: Fanon explicitly rejects replacing colonial owners with a corrupt state bureaucracy; communal ownership need not mean central administration of every firm.

axes.evidence: Independent productive development and escape from raw-material dependence favour selective protection.
axes.counterEvidence: International solidarity and technical exchange remain valuable; tariffs and online-service rules are less specified than rejecting neo-colonial dependency.

axes.evidence: Popular planning and cooperative development should build productive capacity rather than enrich intermediaries.
axes.counterEvidence: Decentralised cooperatives and initiative qualify rigid compulsory central production targets and wage schedules.

axes.evidence: Development should serve the whole population and overcome colonial privilege and concentrated wealth.
axes.counterEvidence: Tax instruments and compensation of former landowners are modern estimates; emancipation is broader than equalising cash incomes.

axes.evidence: Political emancipation and common human membership oppose religious rivalries deciding civil rights.
axes.counterEvidence: Religious community life need not be abolished; festivals and private belief differ from clerical approval of legislation.

axes.evidence: Colonial gender roles and inherited hierarchies can change through participation and liberation.
axes.counterEvidence: Fanon’s treatment of gender and sexuality contains tensions; modern marriage and identity curricula are qualified extensions, not a uniform published programme.

axes.evidence: Productive invention and technical education should replace stagnant colonial economic relations.
axes.counterEvidence: Technological development does not settle every irreversible medical or ecological risk; bounded trials and safety review are inferred.

axes.evidence: The party should be decentralised and regional officials should develop popular participation.
axes.counterEvidence: Fanon also criticises wealthy regional separatism that abandons poorer regions; local authority coexists with national solidarity.

axes.evidence: Colonial social institutions, language and violence shape subjectivity; racial hierarchy is a political construction.
axes.counterEvidence: Individual biological variation is not denied; exact trait proportions are less explicit than the rejection of racial destiny.
